title: Isolating the natural edges of bilayer graphene in gate-defined mesoscopic devices
authors: Francesco Blanda, Grazia Raciti, Thilo Glatzel, Aurin Strathmann, Fabrizio Volante, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ilaria Zardo, Thomas Ihn, Klaus Ensslin, Andrea Hofmann
abstract: We introduce a graphite-gated architecture for bilayer graphene devices in which the active device is completely isolated from the natural graphene edges. Using a single patterned graphite-gate layer, we realize a fully electrostatically defined Hall-bar. Longitudinal and Hall measurements reveal mesoscopic transport features, including Hall-effect quenching and magnetoresistance peaks associated with boundary scattering. The dependence of the mesoscopic features on the carrierdensity shows that the effective channel width increases with the Fermi level and the electrostatic confinement at the gate-defined boundaries, and indicates that the carriers scatter at the electrostatic boundary. Raman spectroscopy and Kelvin probe force microscopy suggest that this boundary is disordered due to the used fabrication methods. Comparably, the quantum mobility in a fieldeffect transistor fabricated with the same architecture is not limited by boundary scattering and the visibility of quantum oscillations down to 4 mT suggests a record value of 2.5 x 10^6 cm2/Vs.
summary: This work reports on the fabrication and characterization of bilayer graphene mesoscopic devices, achieving record quantum mobility by electrostatically isolating the active channel. Furthermore, the study uses KPFM to map surface potentials, demonstrating that substrate plasma treatments critically control the confinement and persistence of injected charge at the graphene/oxide interface.
main_problem: The study aims to isolate and characterize the electronic properties of bilayer graphene (BLG) in mesoscopic devices by eliminating conduction paths through natural flake edges.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that electrostatic definition isolates the active region, yielding high quantum mobility ($\sim 2.5 	imes 10^6 	ext{ cm}^2/	ext{Vs}$) in FET geometries, while also characterizing how substrate treatments affect charge confinement using KPFM.
method: The work combines advanced magnetotransport measurements (Hall-bar and FET) to probe quantum transport with Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy (KPFM) to map local electrostatic potentials after various plasma treatments.
model_or_system: The physical system is bilayer graphene fabricated on various oxide substrates ($	ext{SiO}_2$, plasma-treated $	ext{h-BN}$). Measurements probe mesoscopic transport, Landau quantization, and the electrostatic potential landscape.
key_observables: Quantum mobility ($\mu_q$), quantum lifetime ($	au_q$), Landau level quantization, and Contact Potential Difference ($\Delta V_{	ext{CPD}}$).
important_parameters: Magnetic field ($B$), carrier density ($n$), and plasma treatment type ($	ext{N}_2+	ext{O}_2$ vs. $	ext{CHF}_3/	ext{O}_2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the measured resistance in the gated region is equivalent to the longitudinal resistance in a Corbino geometry for some analyses, and that KPFM measurements can distinguish between intrinsic material potential and trapped surface charges.
figures_summary: Figures show magnetotransport data (Landau fans, $R_{xx}/R_{xy}$ traces) for both FET and Hall-bar geometries, alongside KPFM maps illustrating charge confinement differences on graphene after various plasma treatments.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from demonstrating clean quantum transport in the Hall-bar/FET geometry (magnetotransport) to analyzing edge scattering effects, and finally uses KPFM to investigate the fundamental electrostatic control over the graphene/h-BN interfaces.
why_interesting: The combination of high-precision quantum transport measurements with nanoscale electrostatic characterization (KPFM) provides a comprehensive view of how device fabrication and substrate chemistry dictate fundamental quantum electronic properties in 2D materials.

The Hall-bar gate is separated from the FET gate by a 90 nm-wide gap. c) Atomic force micrograph of the 800 nm-wide FET, in yellow the position of the ohmic contacts.

FIG. 2. Band-gap measurements of the FET. a) Two-terminal resistance as a function of VFET and VBG. The diagonal, highly insulating line appears when the Fermi level lies in the gap opened by the displacement field. Inset: measured current as a function of VBG at a fixed top gate voltage as indicated by the red line. b) Finite bias spectroscopy at fixed displacement field as indicated by the dotted line in a).
FIG. 3. Magnetotransport measurement of the FET at D = 0 V/nm. a) Landau fan from 0 T to 2 T, with the visible filling factors labeled in black. b) Zoom-in of the low field and low density region.

Magnetotransport measuremenet of the Hall-bar at D = 0.1 V / nm. a) Landau fan in Rxx. b) Landau fan in Rxy. c) Low-field trace of Rxx taken at nHall = 1.23 × 1012 cm−2, showing the mesoscopic magnetoresistance peaks. d) Low-field trace of Rxy taken at nHall = 1.23 × 1012 cm−2, showing the quenching of the Hall resistance.
